summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in Croatia since 1977, and open military service is available. Hate-crime legislation covers sexual orientation and gender identity, and the Penal Code equalised the age of consent at 14 in 1998 and raised it to 15 with effect from 1 January 2013. Registered life partnerships have existed since 2014, but a 2013 constitutional referendum barred same-sex marriage. Same-sex couples have obtained family rights only through litigation: the Constitutional Court ruled on 7 February 2020 that excluding same-sex couples from foster care was unconstitutional and discriminatory, Mladen Kožić and Ivo Šegota became Croatia's first same-sex foster parents in September 2020 after a three-year battle, and full adoption rights were confirmed by a final court ruling in 2022.

Legal gender recognition rests on a 2013 legislative amendment that allows a gender marker to be registered without altering sex characteristics. A 2026 analysis in a Croatian legal journal works through the Criminal Procedure Act, the Police Powers Act, the Customs Act and the law governing prison sentences to set out how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming people, and records case studies of the difficulties that arise in practice.

Formal protection outpaces enforcement. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report recorded minority representatives saying that anti-discrimination provisions in employment, housing, education and health are not consistently enforced, NGOs reporting uneven judicial handling of discrimination cases and limited access to justice, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial, and hate-crime investigations judged inadequate. A 2018 Zagreb Pride documentation report on Croatia's implementation of Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 compiled hate-crime data and case studies alongside findings on under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crime, hate speech, freedom of assembly, employment discrimination, legal gender recognition and partnership recognition. A European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination, published in 2024 for the 2023 reporting period, covers transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives including sexual orientation and gender identity grounds.

Hostility is documented in official and public settings. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 records that a session of the Croatian Parliament on 'Gender Ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation with no LGBTI organisations invited, that the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before, and that a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking arising from a 2018 incident. The 2018 Zagreb Pride report further documented hate-speech case studies and constraints on freedom of assembly.

For visitors, a commercial country guide assesses Croatia as widely accepting of LGBTQIA+ travellers but notes that public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less-populated cities and that gay venues are virtually non-existent outside the capital, with new venues appearing in several coastal and regional towns. Community infrastructure includes three LGBT centres, in the capital, in Split (opened 24 May 2014) and in Rijeka (opened 16 October 2014 as LGBTIQ+ Druga Rijeka), alongside Pride marches in Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac and Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March.
tangentialFactors:
Anti-gender mobilisation forms part of the surrounding climate: a 2024 parliamentary session on 'Gender Ideology' platformed misinformation without LGBTI organisations present, and the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before it took place.

In March 2014 Croatia granted asylum for the first time to a person persecuted on the basis of sexual orientation, a young man from Uganda who fled the Anti-Homosexuality Act, which indicates an established protection pathway distinct from tourist entry.

Life partners hold the same health insurance and healthcare rights as married couples under Article 68 of the Life Partnership Act, which prohibits adverse treatment in those areas; the extent to which these rights are recognised for a visiting partner is not addressed by the sources.

Reproductive and preventive healthcare remain unequal: the Medically Supported Fertilization Law limits IVF to married heterosexual couples and single infertile women, effectively excluding same-sex couples, and a 2007 bybylaw places men who have sex with men under categories of permanent rejection for blood donation, framed as of 2021 as 'behaviors or activities that expose them to risk of contracting blood-borne infectious diseases'.

Public opinion recorded in a Eurobarometer-style survey shows 64% of Croatians agreeing that school lessons should include information about sexual orientation diversity and 63% about gender identity, while a 2016 study of children in LGBT families found psychosocial adaptation alongside experiences of stigmatisation.
localsOnly:
Family recognition has advanced by court order rather than statute. As of January 2024 no national law regulates same-sex adoption, protections coming only from court rulings; the Center for Social Welfare initially rejected the Kožić/Šegota foster application twice, and permanent parental rights for a non-biological life partner through partner-guardianship were first secured in July 2015.

An opposition party, Možemo!, proposed in 2023 easier legal gender change and inclusive IVF, and none of those bills had passed as of January 2024.

Community organisation is established on the coast as well as in the capital: the Split LGBT Centre, the second in Croatia and the first in Dalmatia, opened in May 2014 run by the association Risp-et ahead of the fourth Split Pride on 7 June 2014, with organisers demanding equal treatment of same-sex families and Mayor Ivo Baldasar attending the press conference. LGBTIQ+ centre Druga Rijeka was presented in October 2014 to develop the community in Primorsko-goranska county and network with national and international organisations, backed publicly by Mayor Vojko Obersnel and cultural institutions, with goals of visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy.

The largest social scene is in the capital, with clubs, bars and Queer Zagreb programming, and gay-friendly venues and beaches are noted in Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik.

Education materials have been a site of litigation and reform: in 2009 the European Committee on Social Rights found discriminatory statements in a mandatory school biology textbook violating the European Social Charter, and on 1 March 2013 the Minister for Science, Education and Sports announced an action to strip homophobic content from elementary and high school books, especially religious education texts. Youth and family support resources include Zagreb Pride's 2016 guide 'We Have a Family!' and the 2018 picture book 'My Rainbow Family' for preschool-age children with same-sex parents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced: no source in the inventory addresses visa rules, passport gender markers, or entry and border screening procedures for transgender travellers, so what a trans visitor faces on arrival at Croatian passport control is unknown here. The Wikipedia overview is explicit that it says nothing about these matters.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no incident-level reporting on violence against transgender people in Croatia with dates and outcomes; the hate-crime material cited is aggregate or from 2018-era monitoring, and enforcement findings date from the 2021 reporting year.

Unresolved: the relationship between the 2022 final court ruling on same-sex adoption and the absence of a national statute as of January 2024 is stated by the sources at different levels of specificity and is not reconciled here.

Not sourced: whether the 2013 gender-marker amendment has been applied without obstacle in practice beyond the search-procedure case studies in the 2026 legal analysis, and whether blood-donation deferral rules apply to transgender donors specifically rather than to men who have sex with men.
